\section[quid agis? / ut valēs?]{quid agis?, ut valēs? — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}, two genuinely Roman ways}

\label{lesson:LA-C19-quid-agis}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Modern languages often teach one fixed \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} formula. Roman comedy gives you two ordinary questions instead.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
Latin has \textbf{no single fixed idiom} for \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} the way Spanish has \emph{¿cómo estás?} — but it has \textbf{two} genuinely attested colloquial questions, both found repeatedly in \textbf{Plautus} and \textbf{Terence}'s comedies (the closest thing Latin has to recorded everyday speech):

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Quid agis?} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{what are you doing}?\textquotedblright{}, used idiomatically the way English uses \textquotedblleft{}what's up?\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}how's it going?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{Ut valēs?} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{how do you fare}?\textquotedblright{}, built on \textbf{valēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to be strong, to be well\textquotedblright{} — the \textbf{same verb} as \emph{valē}.
\end{itemize}

A third phrase, \textbf{quōmodo tē habēs?} (\textquotedblleft{}how do you hold yourself?\textquotedblright{}), shows up constantly in \textbf{modern} spoken-Latin teaching materials, and it's grammatically perfectly sound — but it is \textbf{not} actually found in any surviving classical text. Be careful with this one: it's a reasonable modern construction, not a Roman one.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}quid agis?\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}what are you doing?\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}ut valēs?\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}how do you fare?\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}quōmodo tē habēs?\textquotedblright{} — grammatical today, but not classically attested{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{quid agis?} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{What are you doing?}\textquotedblright{}) What verb connects \textbf{ut valēs?}, \textbf{valeō}, and the \emph{valē} you already knew from Chapter 1? (\emph{\textbf{Valēre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to be strong/well.\textquotedblright{}) Is \textbf{quōmodo tē habēs?} genuinely attested in classical Latin? (\textbf{No} — grammatically sound, but a modern pedagogical construction, not found in surviving Roman texts.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[valeō, valē]{valeō and valē — answer and farewell from one verb}

\label{lesson:LA-C19-valeo-family}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You can ask \textbf{ut valēs?}, \textquotedblleft{}how do you fare?\textquotedblright{} Its most direct answer is already hiding inside the first farewell you learned.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: valeō — I fare well}
The attested reply is \textbf{valeō}: \textquotedblleft{}I fare well\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}I am strong.\textquotedblright{} Plautus's characters can intensify it as \textbf{valeō rēctē} (\textquotedblleft{}I am properly well\textquotedblright{}) or \textbf{valeō et salvōs sum rēctē} (\textquotedblleft{}I am well and safe\textquotedblright{}).

The dictionary verb is \textbf{valēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to be strong, be well.\textquotedblright{} Watch one stem move through the exchange:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ut valēs?} — how do you fare?
  \item \textbf{valeō} — I fare well
  \item \textbf{valē!} — be well!
\end{itemize}

That last imperative became the Chapter 1 goodbye. Latin's farewell is therefore a wish for the other person to remain well.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}ut valēs?\textquotedblright{} — how do you fare?{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}valeō\textquotedblright{} — I fare well{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}valē\textquotedblright{} — be well; goodbye{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What verb unites \textbf{ut valēs?}, \textbf{valeō}, and \textbf{valē}? (\textbf{Valēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to be strong or well.\textquotedblright{}) Which form answers the question? (\textbf{Valeō.}) What does the farewell \textbf{valē} literally command? (\textbf{Be well.})
\end{tcolorbox}
